method: Questions were researched with an evidence-only retrieval tool over one corpus of open-access and public-domain texts (see corpus.json). Each excerpt was checked word for word against the corpus passage it cites when this file was written; corpus_chunk numbers that passage in the corpus snapshot of 2026-10-01.
questions: What is the classical theory of concepts, and why was it attractive?
What problems does the classical theory face in psychology and philosophy?
What follows for conceptual analysis if concepts lack definitions?

evidence.excerpt: According to the classical theory, a lexical concept C has definitional structure in that it is composed of simpler concepts that express necessary and sufficient conditions for falling under C.
The stock example is the concept BACHELOR, which is traditionally said to have the constituents UNMARRIED and MAN.
Much of its appeal comes from the way it offers unified treatments of concept acquisition, categorization, and reference determination.
Paradigmatic conceptual analyses offer definitions of concepts that are to be tested against potential counterexamples that are identified via thought experiments.
apples are judged to be more typical than plums with respect to the category of fruit
The problem isn’t that the classical theory is inconsistent with results like these but that it does nothing to explain them.
Quite simply, there are too few examples of successful definitional analyses, and certainly none that are uncontroversial
But no one can seem to agree on what the correct definition is.
But another possibility—one that many philosophers are now taking seriously—is that our concepts lack definitional structure.
A radical alternative to all of the theories we’ve mentioned so far is conceptual atomism, the view that lexical concepts have no semantic structure
According to conceptual atomism, the content of a concept isn’t determined by its relation to other concepts but by its relation to the world.
A common theme of this work is that philosophy is supposed to be continuous with science
Others, however, have called into question the connection between conceptual analysis and definitions (Chalmers & Jackson 2001).
The following are correct definitions of Man, according to this test: Man is a mammiferous animal, having (by nature) two hands
Man is an animal who cooks his food: Man is a featherless biped.
